result: Natural variation in C. elegans egg retention was quantified across 316 wild strains, revealing a continuous distribution ranging from approximately 5-50 eggs in utero. The strains were classified into three phenotypic classes: Class I (weak retention, <10 eggs, 15%), Class II (canonical retention, 10-25 eggs, 81%), and Class III (strong retention, >25 eggs, 4%), with several Class III strains exhibiting internal hatching.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are well-supported by quantitative data from 316 strains shown in Figure 1A-C, with clear sample sizes and percentages provided. The classification scheme is empirically derived from the observed distribution, and internal hatching is documented in source data. The measurements appear robust with appropriate sample sizes (N=18-150 per strain).

result: No obvious relationships were found between egg retention phenotypes and geographical/climatic parameters or substrate type. Strains of all three phenotypic classes were found globally and could co-occur in the same locality or microhabitat, though a majority of Class III strains (11/14) were isolated in Europe.
evaluation: Claims C6-C9 are supported by statistical analyses (Spearman correlations, p>0.05) and geographic distribution data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The lack of significant correlations is appropriately reported, though the authors acknowledge potential sampling bias for the European enrichment of Class III strains. The co-occurrence observation is corroborated by previous work (Vigne et al., 2021).

result: GWA mapping identified a single QTL on chromosome III (1.48 Mb) explaining 24% of phenotypic variance in mean egg retention, plus two additional QTL on chromosomes II and IV for variance (CV). Among 257 genes in the main QTL region, five have known roles in egg-laying, but no obvious candidate polymorphisms were detected. The phenotypic distribution and multiple QTL suggest polygenic architecture with multiple common variants.
evaluation: Claims C10-C16 are well-supported by GWA mapping results (Figure 2A-B, Table 1) using appropriate methodology (NemaScan pipeline) with 316 strains. The variance explained (24%) is substantial and the identification of multiple QTL is consistent with polygenic inheritance. The failure to identify obvious candidate polymorphisms (C13) is appropriately reported as a negative result. The QTL do not overlap with hyper-divergent regions, which is informative.

result: Phylogenetic analysis based on whole-genome sequence data indicates that extreme egg retention phenotypes (Class I and III) have evolved multiple times independently. Most Class III strains (13/14) exhibited swept haplotypes, though average egg retention did not differ between divergent and swept strains overall.
evaluation: Claims C17-C19 are supported by phylogenetic analysis using published whole-genome data (Cook et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2021) and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The multiple independent origins of extreme phenotypes is consistent with the polygenic architecture identified by GWA. The observation that most Class III strains have swept haplotypes is interesting but the authors appropriately note this doesn't reflect overall differences between strain types.

result: Among Class III strains, four (including newly isolated NIC1832) carry the KCNL-1 V530L variant, which strongly reduces egg-laying activity and likely arose from a single mutational event based on local haplotype analysis. The remaining 10 Class III strains lacking this variant must have alternative genetic explanations. Natural variation in egg retention is thus shaped by both common variants (from GWA) and multiple rare variants including KCNL-1 V530L.
evaluation: Claims C20-C25 are well-supported by previous work (Vigne et al., 2021) and new phylogenetic analysis (Figure 2C) confirming single origin of KCNL-1 V530L. The identification of a new strain (NIC1832) with this variant strengthens the evidence. The inference that other Class III strains require alternative genetic explanations (C23) is logical given they lack the known variant but exhibit similar phenotypes. The synthesis (C24) appropriately integrates GWA findings (common variants) with rare variant identification.

result: Temporal dynamics of egg number in utero varied strongly across the reproductive span, with all classes showing reduced offspring numbers toward the end of reproduction (mid-L4 +48 to +72 hr). Increased egg retention was linked to prolonged intra-uterine embryonic development, with Class III strains containing more advanced embryonic stages or L1 larvae at mid-L4 +30 hr. Internal hatching occurred consistently in the six strains with highest retention (all Class IIIB and two Class IIIA strains).
evaluation: Claims C27-C31 are well-supported by temporal data (Figure 3C) and embryonic staging data (Figure 3D-E). The observations are consistent with established knowledge about C. elegans reproduction (multiple citations provided). Sample sizes are adequate (N=28-96 per strain per timepoint). The link between egg retention and prolonged embryonic development is directly demonstrated by embryonic age distribution data.

result: Both egg and body size showed significant differences across the 15 focal strains, with a trend for correlation between body and egg size. However, neither egg nor body size correlated with mean egg retention, suggesting that the capacity to retain eggs is not simply a function of body or egg size.
evaluation: Claims C32-C35 are supported by morphometric data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-F). The statistical analyses appropriately test for correlations, and the lack of correlation between size measures and egg retention (C34) is clearly shown. The inference that egg retention capacity is not simply size-dependent (C35) is reasonable given the data, though other unmeasured factors could still be involved.

result: Egg-laying activity was highly dynamic, peaking between mid-L4 +24-30 hr for most strains. Class III strains exhibited shortened egg-laying windows. The number of intervals with egg laying varied significantly between strains and classes, with Class I showing increased and Class IIIB showing reduced intervals. Strains with strong retention exhibited prolonged inactive periods. The N2 reference strain expelled significantly more eggs per interval than all other strains, likely due to its specific npr-1 allele. Overall, strain and class differences in egg-laying behavior partly align with egg retention differences.
evaluation: Claims C36-C44 are well-supported by behavioral data (Figures 4-5) with appropriate sample sizes (N=17-18 per strain). The scan-sampling method is clearly described and appropriate for detecting variation in egg-laying patterns, though it lacks the resolution of continuous video imaging. Statistical analyses (Two-Way ANOVA) are appropriate. The N2 phenotype attribution to npr-1 (C43) is supported by comparison with QX1430 (npr-1 corrected strain). The synthesis (C44) appropriately notes partial alignment, acknowledging complexity.

result: Class II strains laid their first egg after accumulating ~5-10 eggs in utero (~1-2 hr after fertilization), consistent with previous N2 reports. Class I and III strains showed significantly advanced and delayed first egg-laying events, respectively. A substantial portion of natural variation in egg retention can be attributed to differences in egg-laying behavior, particularly through differential delay of the first egg-laying event. The sensitivity to mechanosensory stimuli triggering egg-laying onset appears to vary across strains, potentially representing a principal mechanism driving variation. More subtle differences in behavioral phenotypes at peak activity also correlated with retention differences.
evaluation: Claims C45-C52 are well-supported by behavioral data (Figure 6A-B) with adequate sample sizes (N=16-22 per strain). The timing measurements are consistent with previous work (Ravi et al., 2018). The inference about mechanosensory perception (C49-C50) is reasonable given established knowledge about egg-laying regulation (multiple citations), though C50 is somewhat speculative. The synthesis (C52) appropriately integrates findings showing variation manifests at multiple timepoints during adulthood.

result: Observed strain differences in egg-laying behavior potentially arise through genetic variation in the neuromodulatory architecture of the egg-laying circuit, where serotonin plays a central role. Exposure to high-dose serotonin (25 mM) consistently increased egg laying in Class I and II strains but showed highly variable responses in Class III strains. Among Class IIIA strains, serotonin stimulated egg laying in all except JU2829 (where it inhibited), and induced much stronger responses in ED3005 (possible hypersensitivity). Class IIIB strains showed no effect or inhibition. Strains within Classes I, II, and IIIA showed subtle but significant quantitative differences in serotonin response. Stimulation by exogenous serotonin was strongly genotype-dependent, indicating genetic differences in neuromodulatory architecture contribute to natural diversity in egg-laying behavior.
evaluation: Claims C53-C62 are well-supported by pharmacological assay data (Figure 7B) with appropriate sample sizes (N=11-24 replicates per strain). The experimental design (liquid M9 assay) is standard for C. elegans egg-laying studies. Statistical analyses (Align Rank Transform ANOVA) are appropriate for the data. The variable responses across strains, particularly the inhibitory effects in some Class III strains, are clearly demonstrated. The inference about genetic variation in neuromodulatory architecture (C62) is well-supported by the genotype-dependent responses. C53 and C58 are somewhat speculative but reasonable given the data.

result: Fluoxetine and imipramine strongly stimulated egg-laying in all 15 focal strains, including Class IIIB strains and JU2829 (Class IIIA) where serotonin had no effect or inhibited egg laying. Based on previous interpretations of mutants unresponsive to serotonin but responsive to these drugs, Class IIIB strains are likely defective in vulval muscle activation via serotonin, and JU2829 may exhibit a similar defect from an alternative genetic change. The pharmacological assays do not allow conclusions about HSN function divergence, but results are consistent with previous models proposing these drugs can stimulate egg laying through mechanisms independent of serotonergic signaling.
evaluation: Claims C63-C69 are supported by pharmacological data (Figure 7B) showing consistent drug responses across strains. The interpretation draws appropriately on established knowledge from mutant studies (multiple citations). The inference about Class IIIB defects (C66) is reasonable given the known function of KCNL-1 V530L. The speculation about JU2829 (C67) is logical based on similar response patterns but remains to be validated. The acknowledgment of limitations (C68) is appropriate. The consistency with previous models (C69) is well-supported by multiple citations.

result: Serotonin inhibited egg laying in JU2829 (Class IIIA) and showed similar tendencies in Class IIIB strains, consistent with past research on dual serotonin signaling (excitatory and inhibitory). In N2, inhibitory inputs are masked by stronger excitatory inputs and only revealed when serotonin receptors are mutationally disrupted. The KCNL-1 V530L variant likely hyperpolarizes vulval muscles such that exogenous serotonin is insufficient for egg laying while negative inputs can exert effects. CRISPR experiments introducing V530L into JU1200 recapitulated the inhibitory serotonin response, while introducing canonical KCNL-1 into JU751 restored normal responses. Both fluoxetine and imipramine stimulated egg laying in engineered strains. These results confirm that variation in a single amino acid residue of KCNL-1 is sufficient to explain drastic differences in the egg-laying system and its response to neuromodulatory inputs.
evaluation: Claims C70-C78 are strongly supported by pharmacological data (Figure 7B-C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and CRISPR validation experiments. The CRISPR approach provides causal evidence that KCNL-1 V530L is sufficient to alter neuromodulatory responses (C75, C77, C78). The interpretation draws appropriately on established knowledge about dual serotonin signaling (C71-C72, multiple citations). The mechanistic explanation (C74) is reasonable given known KCNL-1 function. The reciprocal CRISPR experiments (introducing and removing the variant) provide strong validation.

result: Introduction of mod-5(n822) loss-of-function mutation (increasing endogenous serotonin) into 10 wild strains showed genotype-dependent effects on egg-laying activity. Several strains did not show significantly increased responses. The effect was quantitatively different for strains within the same phenotypic class, indicating serotonin sensitivity varies genetically despite similar behavioral outputs. At high serotonin doses (25 mM), mod-5(lf) had no additional effect (except ED3005), but lower concentrations uncovered significant strain differences in sensitivity that were contingent on mod-5(lf) presence. These genotype-dependent effect sizes provide evidence for epistasis. C. elegans harbors natural variation in genetic architecture affecting sensitivity to neuromodulatory inputs, which can occur in egg-laying circuit elements (like KCNL-1 V530L) but likely also in components outside the core circuit.
evaluation: Claims C79-C90 are well-supported by CRISPR-engineered strain data (Figure 8, Table 3) with appropriate sample sizes and statistical analyses (ANOVA showing significant interactions). The epistatic interpretation (C88) is appropriate given significant genotype x treatment interactions. The experimental design systematically tests the same genetic perturbation across multiple backgrounds, providing strong evidence for genetic architecture variation (C89). The speculation about variation outside the core circuit (C90) is reasonable but remains to be validated. The dose-response experiments (C82-C85) effectively demonstrate context-dependent effects.

result: Strains with stronger egg retention showed reduced lifetime self-fertility and survival, with strongest reductions in Class IIIB strains. Class III strains showed frequent internal hatching with premature maternal death, sometimes before reproduction ended, while Class I and II strains showed absent or rare internal hatching only at the end of reproduction. A fraction of Class III adults had remaining self-sperm at internal hatching, confirming it can occur during the reproductive span and potentially disrupt self-fertilization. In JU2593 (Class IIIB), total self-sperm greatly exceeded lifetime progeny. Internally hatched larvae caused physical damage to maternal gonad and soma, and larval movement scattered sperm away from spermathecae, likely reducing fertilization efficacy. Strong egg retention and internal hatching correlate with reduced self-fertility and maternal survival. Class IIIB strains exhibited the most drastic reduction in reproductive output, using only a fraction of available self-sperm. In contrast, Class IIIA strains (ED3005, JU440, NIC1786) showed internal hatching mainly after reproduction ceased, suggesting limited detrimental fitness effects.
evaluation: Claims C91-C102 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: lifetime fertility data (Figure 9A-C), survival data (Figure 10A-C), and sperm/internal hatching analyses (Figure 11, Figure 11—figure supplement 1). Sample sizes are adequate (N=28-30 for fertility, N=90-102 for survival, N=45-193 for DAPI staining). The correlations between egg retention and fitness costs are clearly demonstrated. The mechanistic observations about physical damage and sperm scattering (C97-C98) are supported by microscopy data. The distinction between Class IIIA and IIIB fitness effects (C102) is important and well-supported.

result: Strong egg retention reflects prolonged intra-uterine embryonic development, resulting in laying of eggs with advanced-stage embryos. Class I and II strains laid eggs with embryos rarely exceeding the 26-cell stage, while Class III laid eggs with differentiated embryos containing hundreds of cells, sometimes close to hatching. These differences are considerable in the context of C. elegans' rapid life cycle (~80 hr egg-to-adult), representing ~2-3 hr vs ~9-12 hr of development. Prolonged retention should result in earlier hatching ex utero, potentially affecting competitive fitness. Eggs of Class IIIB strains and some Class IIIA strains hatched ~2-5 hours earlier than Class I and II strains. Many Class III strains reached reproductive maturity ~2-6 hr earlier, though some did not maintain their initial head start. Overall, strains with prolonged egg retention benefit from relatively shorter developmental time from laying to maturity, which might improve competitive ability.
evaluation: Claims C103-C110 are well-supported by embryonic staging data (Figure 12A), hatching time measurements (Figure 12B), and developmental time data (Figure 12C) with adequate sample sizes (N=45-72 eggs for staging, N=48-177 eggs for hatching, N=77-318 eggs for development). The developmental timing information (C105) draws appropriately on established knowledge (Hall and Altun, 2007). The speculation about competitive fitness (C106-C107, C110) is reasonable but requires experimental validation. The observation that some Class III strains don't maintain their head start (C109) is important and appropriately reported.

result: In competition experiments, the KCNL-1 V530L variant (JU1200KCNL-1 V530L) performed significantly better than wild-type JU1200 against a GFP-tester strain at food exhaustion (~5 days). Given that the principal phenotypic effect of KCNL-1 V530L is increased egg retention, strong egg retention can improve competitive ability in food-limited environments. In direct competition between JU751 (Class IIIB) and five strains from the same habitat, JU751 reached higher adult population sizes at food exhaustion in all five cases. These results offer preliminary evidence that laying advanced-stage embryos may enhance intraspecific competitive ability, particularly when multiple genotypes compete for limited, patchily distributed resources. Previous work showed increased egg-to-adult developmental time is disadvantageous for C. elegans population growth when resources are limited. Together with evidence from insects, these observations indicate maternal features accelerating offspring development after oviposition can confer fitness benefits in ephemeral habitats with rapidly decaying resources.
evaluation: Claims C111-C116 are supported by competition experiment data (Figure 12D-E) with adequate replication (N=10 per genotype). The experimental design appropriately tests competitive ability under resource limitation. The inference that egg retention improves competitive ability (C112) is reasonable given the CRISPR-controlled comparison, though the authors appropriately note the analysis is centered on a single genetic background (C114). The integration with previous C. elegans work (C115) and evidence from other taxa (C116) strengthens the interpretation. However, the mechanism (earlier hatching vs. other factors) could be more directly tested.

result: Prolonged intra-uterine embryonic development in viviparous organisms is thought to provide improved protection against environmental fluctuations and stressors. Whether prolonged egg retention in C. elegans increases such protection is unclear because embryos are already well-protected by a multi-layered egg shell highly resistant to diverse environmental insults. Nevertheless, eggs developing ex utero are still vulnerable to various abiotic and biotic stressors. If eggs in utero are more effectively shielded than eggs laid externally, genotypes with strong egg retention may benefit from improved offspring protection.
evaluation: Claims C117-C120 appropriately frame the hypothesis to be tested by drawing on established evolutionary theory (C117, multiple citations) and known properties of C. elegans egg shells (C118-C119, multiple citations). The hypothesis (C120) is clearly speculative and appropriately framed as such. This sets up the subsequent experimental tests of offspring protection.

result: Across strains, most eggs removed from mothers and directly exposed to high concentrations of ethanol (96%) and acetic acid (10 M) were killed, whereas eggs inside mothers exhibited significantly higher survival, particularly for acetic acid. Eggs in utero were partly protected by the mother's body, even though mothers died instantly. Consequently, increased egg retention resulted in higher numbers of surviving offspring per mother in both stress treatments. Exposure to acetic acid confirmed that higher egg retention of JU751 increased surviving offspring compared to strains with lower retention. The number of surviving offspring in JU1200WT (~15 eggs) was much reduced compared to JU1200KCNL-1 V530L (~40 eggs) when exposed to acetic acid. Larvae in utero were also efficiently protected. Offspring in utero may benefit from maternal protection, so strains with constitutively higher egg retention will protect more progeny when confronting sudden environmental insults.
evaluation: Claims C121-C127 are well-supported by stress exposure experiments (Figures 13-14) with adequate replication (N=5-10 replicates per treatment). The experimental design appropriately compares eggs ex utero vs. in utero. The CRISPR-controlled comparison (C125) provides strong evidence that egg retention per se (not other genetic differences) confers protection. The observation that mothers die instantly (C122) is important for interpreting the protection mechanism. The inference about maternal protection (C127) is well-supported by the data.

result: Fertility of individuals derived from stress-exposed eggs ex utero was reduced compared to those from eggs in utero when exposed to osmotic stress (0.3 M NaCl). Individuals from ex utero eggs exposed to low concentration acetic acid (1 M) developed more slowly and exhibited significantly delayed reproductive maturity (but not reduced fertility) compared to those from eggs in utero. Larvae in utero at stress exposure were protected and produced as many offspring as controls, while larvae exposed ex utero were killed instantly. Together, these results suggest constitutively strong egg retention can enhance maternal protection by protecting more eggs in utero when facing sudden environmental perturbations. Prolonged egg retention will also reduce total external exposure time of the immobile embryonic stage, likely lowering risks from diverse environmental threats including predators and pathogens.
evaluation: Claims C128-C133 are supported by stress exposure experiments with fitness measurements (Figure 15) with adequate sample sizes (N=15-22 per treatment). The experimental design appropriately tests both survival and subsequent fitness of stress-exposed offspring. The observation that larvae in utero are protected while those ex utero are killed (C130-C131) is striking. The synthesis (C132) is well-supported by the data. The speculation about reduced exposure to predators and pathogens (C133) is reasonable but remains to be tested.

result: The degree of C. elegans egg retention alters the interplay of antagonistic effects on maternal versus offspring fitness. Strong egg retention reduces maternal survival and reproduction, but by prolonging intra-uterine embryonic development, offspring may benefit from improved competitive ability and protection against environmental insults. Variable egg retention in natural populations may reflect genetic differences in the adjustment of an intergenerational fitness trade-off. In extreme cases, C. elegans strains exhibit partial viviparity associated with significantly reduced maternal reproduction and survival. Observed genetically variable duration of intra-uterine development aligns well with reports showing transitions towards viviparity incur maternal fitness costs across diverse taxa. Given the nearly exclusive selfing mode of C. elegans reproduction, there is expected to be little genetic disparity between mothers and offspring, indicating reduced opportunities for intergenerational conflict. Observed natural differences in egg retention are predicted to reflect properties of genetically distinct genotypes, likely resulting from adaptation to distinct ecological niches differing in resource availability.
evaluation: Claims C134-C140 synthesize the major findings of the study. The evidence for antagonistic effects on maternal vs. offspring fitness (C134-C135) is well-supported by the experimental data presented throughout. The interpretation as an intergenerational fitness trade-off (C136) is reasonable given the data. The alignment with previous work on viviparity costs (C138) is appropriate and well-cited. The inference about reduced intergenerational conflict due to selfing (C139) is logical and draws on established evolutionary theory. The speculation about ecological adaptation (C140) is reasonable but remains to be tested. Overall, this synthesis appropriately integrates the findings while acknowledging limitations and uncertainties.
